claim: Core nuclear functions, including transcription, replication, and heterochromatin formation, occur in spatially restricted clusters.
source: Modern microscopy has revealed that core nuclear functions, including transcription, replication, and heterochromatin formation, occur in spatially restricted clusters.
evidence: This is a general statement about nuclear organization supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Subnuclear high-concentration clusters of transcription factors may play a role in regulating RNA synthesis in the early Drosophila embryo.
source: Previous work from our lab has shown that subnuclear high-concentration clusters of transcription factors may play a role in regulating RNA synthesis in the early Drosophila embryo.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work from the authors' lab.

claim: Eukaryotic transcription factors contain intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) that often arise from low complexity amino acid sequences within the protein.
source: A nearly ubiquitous feature of eukaryotic transcription factors is that they contain intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) that often arise from low complexity amino acid sequences within the protein.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of transcription factors in the scientific literature.

claim: It has been proposed that IDRs within transcription factors drive co-localization of transcriptional machinery and target genes into high-concentration clusters within nuclei.
source: It has been proposed that IDRs within transcription factors drive co-localization of transcriptional machinery and target genes into high-concentration clusters within nuclei.
evidence: This claim references a hypothesis from the literature.

claim: Subnuclear clustering does not occur when the majority of IDRs are expressed alone.
source: We found that while subnuclear clustering does not occur when the majority of IDRs are expressed alone, it is frequently seen in full-length transcription factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the high-throughput imaging screen described in the manuscript.

claim: Subnuclear clustering is frequently seen in full-length transcription factors.
source: We found that while subnuclear clustering does not occur when the majority of IDRs are expressed alone, it is frequently seen in full-length transcription factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental imaging data of full-length transcription factors in the manuscript.

claim: IDRs are insufficient to drive the subnuclear clustering behavior of transcription factors.
source: These results are consistent in live Drosophila embryos, suggesting that IDRs are insufficient to drive the subnuclear clustering behavior of transcription factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from both S2 cells and live embryos showing that IDRs alone do not cluster.

claim: The clustering of transcription factors in living embryos was unaffected by the deletion of IDR sequences.
source: Furthermore, the clustering of transcription factors in living embryos was unaffected by the deletion of IDR sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from IDR deletion constructs imaged in embryos.

claim: IDRs are unlikely to be the primary molecular drivers of the clustering observed during transcription.
source: Our results demonstrate that IDRs are unlikely to be the primary molecular drivers of the clustering observed during transcription, suggesting a more complex and nuanced role for these disordered protein sequences.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing IDRs are neither necessary nor sufficient for clustering.

claim: Gene expression requires the coordinated assembly of transcriptional machinery at specific sites in the genome.
source: Gene expression is a tightly regulated process that requires the coordinated assembly of transcriptional machinery at specific sites in the genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gene expression mechanisms.

claim: Gene expression depends on interactions between sequence-specific DNA-binding transcription factors at enhancer sequences, general TFs, and co-activators including the Mediator complex, and RNA polymerase II (PolII) at promoters.
source: This process depends on interactions between sequence-specific DNA-binding transcription factors (TFs) at enhancer sequences, general TFs, and co-activators including the Mediator complex, and RNA polymerase II (PolII) at promoters (Reiter et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Reiter et al., 2017.

claim: Classical models of transcription describe a mechanism in which TFs bound at distant enhancers are able to communicate with PolII at the promoter via chromatin looping.
source: Classical models of transcription describe a mechanism in which TFs bound at distant enhancers are able to communicate with PolII at the promoter via chromatin looping (Su et al., 1991), and there is ample biochemical and genetic evidence for this process (Kornberg, 2005; Krivega and Dean, 2012; Robinson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing chromatin looping models.

claim: There is ample biochemical and genetic evidence for chromatin looping in transcription.
source: Classical models of transcription describe a mechanism in which TFs bound at distant enhancers are able to communicate with PolII at the promoter via chromatin looping (Su et al., 1991), and there is ample biochemical and genetic evidence for this process (Kornberg, 2005; Krivega and Dean, 2012; Robinson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kornberg, 2005; Krivega and Dean, 2012; Robinson et al., 2016.

claim: Eukaryotic TFs share common structural components, having at minimum a sequence-specific DNA-binding domain and transcriptional activation domain.
source: Eukaryotic TFs share common structural components, having at minimum a sequence-specific DNA-binding domain and transcriptional activation domain (Brent and Ptashne, 1985; Kadonaga et al., 1988; Keegan et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brent and Ptashne, 1985; Kadonaga et al., 1988; Keegan et al., 1986.

claim: The DNA-binding domains of TFs are typically folded into a defined structure.
source: While the DNA-binding domains of TFs are typically folded into a defined structure, regions of the protein outside of the DNA-binding domain, including transcriptional activation domains, often remain flexible or unstructured (Guo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2012 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Regions of the protein outside of the DNA-binding domain, including transcriptional activation domains, often remain flexible or unstructured.
source: While the DNA-binding domains of TFs are typically folded into a defined structure, regions of the protein outside of the DNA-binding domain, including transcriptional activation domains, often remain flexible or unstructured (Guo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2012.

claim: Intrinsically disordered regions often have lower complexity in their amino acid sequence than structured domains.
source: These intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), which often have lower complexity in their amino acid sequence than structured domains, are highly overrepresented in eukaryotic TFs and essential for their function (Liu et al., 2006; Minezaki et al., 2006; Staby et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about IDR characteristics supported by citations.

claim: IDRs are highly overrepresented in eukaryotic TFs and essential for their function.
source: These intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), which often have lower complexity in their amino acid sequence than structured domains, are highly overrepresented in eukaryotic TFs and essential for their function (Liu et al., 2006; Minezaki et al., 2006; Staby et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2006; Minezaki et al., 2006; Staby et al., 2017.

claim: Single-molecule imaging of PolII shows that it forms transient clusters containing multiple active polymerases which are associated with active transcription at individual loci.
source: Single-molecule imaging of PolII, for example, shows that it forms transient clusters containing multiple active polymerases which are associated with active transcription at individual loci (Cisse et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cisse et al., 2013.

claim: Localized regions of active transcription arise from interactions between the repeat-rich carboxy-terminal domain of the RBP1 subunit of PolII and the activation domains of TFs that contain IDRs with low sequence complexity.
source: Biochemical studies suggest that localized regions of active transcription arise from interactions between the repeat-rich carboxy-terminal domain of the RBP1 subunit of PolII and the activation domains of TFs that contain IDRs with low sequence complexity.
evidence: This claim is based on biochemical studies referenced in the text.

claim: IDRs from transcription factors can be polymerized into gel-like droplets, which can bind to PolII in vitro.
source: These IDRs can be polymerized into gel-like droplets, which can bind to PolII in vitro (Kwon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kwon et al., 2013.

claim: The embryonic stem cell pluripotency factor Sox2 forms transient clusters at the enhancers of its target genes in living cells.
source: The embryonic stem cell pluripotency factor Sox2 has been shown to form transient clusters at the enhancers of its target genes in living cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014 (implied from context).

claim: Sox2 cluster formation is mediated by weak protein-protein interactions between unstructured, low complexity sequences in the Sox2 activation domain.
source: It was proposed that cluster formation is mediated by weak protein-protein interactions between unstructured, low complexity sequences in the Sox2 activation domain, and that these clusters create high local concentrations of TFs and possibly associated co-factors to create hubs of gene activation (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014.

claim: Sox2 clusters create high local concentrations of TFs and possibly associated co-factors to create hubs of gene activation.
source: It was proposed that cluster formation is mediated by weak protein-protein interactions between unstructured, low complexity sequences in the Sox2 activation domain, and that these clusters create high local concentrations of TFs and possibly associated co-factors to create hubs of gene activation (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2014.

claim: IDRs within TFs mediate interactions with PolII in dynamic, high-concentration multi-protein hubs that activate transcription in human cells.
source: IDRs within TFs have also been demonstrated to mediate interactions with PolII in dynamic, high-concentration multi-protein hubs that activate transcription in human cells (Chong et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chong et al., 2018.

claim: PolII and Mediator form dynamic clusters in living cells that can co-localize within the nucleus.
source: PolII and Mediator have also been shown to form dynamic clusters in living cells that can co-localize within the nucleus (Cho et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cho et al., 2018.

claim: Mediator can form phase-separated condensates with the human TFs OCT4 and GCN4 in vitro.
source: Biochemical evidence also demonstrates that Mediator can form phase-separated condensates with the human TFs OCT4 and GCN4 in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical evidence referenced in the text.

claim: The formation of Mediator condensates with OCT4 and GCN4 requires the intrinsically disordered activation domains of the TFs.
source: The formation of these condensates requires the intrinsically disordered activation domains of the TFs, which are also necessary for transcriptional activation in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical evidence from Boija et al., 2018 (implied from context).

claim: The intrinsically disordered activation domains of OCT4 and GCN4 are necessary for transcriptional activation in vivo.
source: The formation of these condensates requires the intrinsically disordered activation domains of the TFs, which are also necessary for transcriptional activation in vivo. These findings indicate that gene activation is driven by dynamic, low affinity interactions between TFs and co-factors at enhancers (Boija et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Boija et al., 2018.

claim: Gene activation is driven by dynamic, low affinity interactions between TFs and co-factors at enhancers.
source: These findings indicate that gene activation is driven by dynamic, low affinity interactions between TFs and co-factors at enhancers (Boija et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Boija et al., 2018.

claim: Two maternally provided TFs, Bicoid and Zelda, form hubs of high local concentration within nuclei in developing Drosophila embryos.
source: Work from our own lab has demonstrated that two maternally provided TFs, Bicoid and Zelda, form hubs of high local concentration within nuclei in developing Drosophila embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to work from the authors' lab.

claim: Bicoid and Zelda hubs are highly dynamic and interact transiently with sites of transcription.
source: These hubs are highly dynamic and interact transiently with sites of transcription (Mir et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mir et al., 2018.

claim: Both Bicoid and Zelda are predicted to contain significant intrinsic disorder.
source: Although both proteins are predicted to contain significant intrinsic disorder, with Zelda being particularly disordered (Hamm et al., 2015), it is unclear to what degree IDRs influence their dynamics in the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hamm et al., 2015.

claim: Zelda is particularly disordered compared to Bicoid.
source: Although both proteins are predicted to contain significant intrinsic disorder, with Zelda being particularly disordered (Hamm et al., 2015), it is unclear to what degree IDRs influence their dynamics in the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hamm et al., 2015.

claim: IUPred predicts disordered regions from an amino acid sequence by estimating the ability of polypeptides to form stabilizing contacts.
source: We started with an existing disorder predictor, IUPred, which predicts disordered regions from an amino acid sequence by estimating the ability of polypeptides to form stabilizing contacts (Dosztányi et al., 2005; Mészáros et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dosztányi et al., 2005; Mészáros et al., 2018.

claim: IUPred scores were lower (indicating less predicted disorder) in structured domains than in sequences outside of these domains.
source: We found that, as expected, IUPred scores were lower (indicating less predicted disorder) in structured domains than in sequences outside of these domains (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The HMM successfully predicts a structured region corresponding to the basic helix-loop-helix DNA-binding domain in daughterless protein.
source: This protein is known to contain a basic helix-loop-helix DNA-binding domain (Gebali et al., 2019; Letunic et al., 2015; Murre et al., 1989), and our HMM successfully predicts a structured region corresponding to this domain and three continuous unstructured regions in the rest of the protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the HMM prediction and citations about the daughterless protein structure.

claim: The HMM predicts three continuous unstructured regions in the daughterless protein outside of the DNA-binding domain.
source: This protein is known to contain a basic helix-loop-helix DNA-binding domain (Gebali et al., 2019; Letunic et al., 2015; Murre et al., 1989), and our HMM successfully predicts a structured region corresponding to this domain and three continuous unstructured regions in the rest of the protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the HMM prediction shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There was a strong enrichment for predicted structured sequence from the HMM model in known Pfam/SMART domains.
source: There was a strong enrichment for predicted structured sequence from our model in known Pfam/SMART domains and a strong depletion of predicted unstructured sequence in the same domains, relative to the rest of the proteome (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was a strong depletion of predicted unstructured sequence in known Pfam/SMART domains, relative to the rest of the proteome.
source: There was a strong enrichment for predicted structured sequence from our model in known Pfam/SMART domains and a strong depletion of predicted unstructured sequence in the same domains, relative to the rest of the proteome (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The HMM can successfully predict disorder from the proteome while largely excluding structured domains.
source: This result demonstrates that our HMM can successfully predict disorder from the proteome while largely excluding structured domains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The HMM Viterbi calls generally agree with existing annotations of IDRs in the MobiDB protein disorder database.
source: Additionally, our Viterbi calls generally agree with existing annotations of IDRs, when checked against the MobiDB protein disorder database (Di Domenico et al., 2012; Coronado et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with the MobiDB database, cited as Di Domenico et al., 2012; Coronado et al., 2021.

claim: The final IDR library contained 75 IDRs.
source: We were unable to amplify 3 of the IDRs from the genome, so the final library contained 75 IDRs.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental library.

claim: Nearly all of the IDRs were distributed homogeneously within the nucleus in S2 cells.
source: High-throughput imaging of live cells revealed that nearly all of the IDRs were distributed homogeneously within the nucleus (Figure 2A), suggesting that IDRs alone are insufficient to drive subnuclear clustering behavior of the type that we observe in TFs in the embryo.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Two of the 75 IDRs were sufficient to drive clustering in S2 Cells: IDR16 from the protein MESR4 and IDR72 from the protein Brk.
source: Two of the 75 IDRs were sufficient to drive clustering in S2 Cells: IDR16 from the protein MESR4 (misexpression suppressor of ras 4) and IDR72 from the protein Brk (brinker).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The MESR4 IDR has several large, bright clusters throughout the nucleus in S2 cells.
source: Both IDRs show non-uniform nuclear distribution, with the MESR4 IDR having several large, bright clusters throughout the nucleus, and the Brk IDR showing more fine-scale clustering (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Brk IDR shows fine-scale clustering in S2 cells.
source: Both IDRs show non-uniform nuclear distribution, with the MESR4 IDR having several large, bright clusters throughout the nucleus, and the Brk IDR showing more fine-scale clustering (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MESR4 was first identified for playing a role in the RAS1 signaling pathway.
source: MESR4 was first identified for playing a role in the RAS1 signaling pathway (Huang and Rubin, 2000) and has since been identified in several genetic screens, with roles in lipid metabolism and gene regulation (Tsuda-Sakurai et al., 2015), cellular responses to hypoxia (Lee et al., 2008), and germline differentiation (Wissel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Huang and Rubin, 2000.

claim: MESR4 has roles in lipid metabolism and gene regulation.
source: MESR4 was first identified for playing a role in the RAS1 signaling pathway (Huang and Rubin, 2000) and has since been identified in several genetic screens, with roles in lipid metabolism and gene regulation (Tsuda-Sakurai et al., 2015), cellular responses to hypoxia (Lee et al., 2008), and germline differentiation (Wissel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tsuda-Sakurai et al., 2015.

claim: MESR4 has roles in cellular responses to hypoxia.
source: MESR4 was first identified for playing a role in the RAS1 signaling pathway (Huang and Rubin, 2000) and has since been identified in several genetic screens, with roles in lipid metabolism and gene regulation (Tsuda-Sakurai et al., 2015), cellular responses to hypoxia (Lee et al., 2008), and germline differentiation (Wissel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2008.

claim: MESR4 has roles in germline differentiation.
source: MESR4 was first identified for playing a role in the RAS1 signaling pathway (Huang and Rubin, 2000) and has since been identified in several genetic screens, with roles in lipid metabolism and gene regulation (Tsuda-Sakurai et al., 2015), cellular responses to hypoxia (Lee et al., 2008), and germline differentiation (Wissel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wissel et al., 2016.

claim: The full-length MESR4 protein contains nine C2H2-type zinc fingers and a plant homeodomain-type zinc finger.
source: The full-length protein contains nine C2H2-type zinc fingers and a plant homeodomain-type zinc finger (Letunic et al., 2015; Schultz et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Letunic et al., 2015; Schultz et al., 1998.

claim: MESR4 was identified as a component of the histone locus body (HLB).
source: Interestingly, it was also identified as a component of the histone locus body (HLB), a nuclear compartment that serves as a site of histone synthesis (White et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to White et al., 2011.

claim: The HLB is a nuclear compartment that serves as a site of histone synthesis.
source: Interestingly, it was also identified as a component of the histone locus body (HLB), a nuclear compartment that serves as a site of histone synthesis (White et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to White et al., 2011.

claim: HLB localization likely does not explain the clustering observed for the MESR4 IDR.
source: However, as the HLB appears as a single bright spot in the nucleus of S2 cells, HLB localization likely does not explain the clustering observed for the MESR4 IDR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the MESR4 IDR shows multiple clusters rather than a single spot.

claim: Brk is a transcriptional repressor that is negatively regulated by Dpp signaling in the embryo and the larval imaginal discs.
source: Brk is a transcriptional repressor that is negatively regulated by Dpp signaling in the embryo and the larval imaginal discs (Jaźwińska et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jaźwińska et al., 1999.

claim: The Brinker DNA-binding domain is unstructured and flexible in the absence of DNA, but folds upon DNA-binding.
source: The protein contains a Brinker DNA-binding domain, which has been shown to be unstructured and flexible in the absence of DNA, but to fold upon DNA-binding (Cordier et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cordier et al., 2006.

claim: The DNA-binding domain of Brk is contained entirely within the IDR expressed in the study.
source: The DNA-binding domain is contained entirely within the IDR expressed in our study, which raises the possibility that the observed clustering of this IDR is the result of the tagged protein fragment binding to DNA in S2 cells.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the IDR construct used in the study.

claim: The observed clustering of the Brk IDR may be the result of the tagged protein fragment binding to DNA in S2 cells.
source: The DNA-binding domain is contained entirely within the IDR expressed in our study, which raises the possibility that the observed clustering of this IDR is the result of the tagged protein fragment binding to DNA in S2 cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the presence of the DNA-binding domain in the IDR.

claim: IDR13 from CG42748 localizes to both the nucleus and the plasma membrane.
source: For example, IDR13 is from the protein encoded by CG42748, which is predicted to be involved in the organization of cell-cell junctions (Lye et al., 2014), and localizes to both the nucleus and the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CG42748 is predicted to be involved in the organization of cell-cell junctions.
source: For example, IDR13 is from the protein encoded by CG42748, which is predicted to be involved in the organization of cell-cell junctions (Lye et al., 2014), and localizes to both the nucleus and the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lye et al., 2014.

claim: IDR31 from CG7839 is strongly localized to the nucleolus.
source: IDR31 appears to be strongly localized to the nucleolus.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CG7839 contains a CCAAT binding factor domain.
source: This IDR is from the largely uncharacterized protein encoded by CG7839, which contains a CCAAT binding factor domain (Blum et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Blum et al., 2021.

claim: The CCAAT binding factor domain is found in proteins known to play a role in 60S ribosomal subunit biogenesis in yeast.
source: This domain is found in proteins known to play a role in 60S ribosomal subunit biogenesis in yeast (Edskes et al., 1998) and regulating hsp70 expression in humans (Lum et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Edskes et al., 1998.

claim: The CCAAT binding factor domain is found in proteins that regulate hsp70 expression in humans.
source: This domain is found in proteins known to play a role in 60S ribosomal subunit biogenesis in yeast (Edskes et al., 1998) and regulating hsp70 expression in humans (Lum et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lum et al., 1990.

claim: Some of the IDRs retain some degree of function or nuclear addressing that would be expected from the full-length protein.
source: The localization patterns observed in S2 cells indicate that some of the IDRs retain some degree of function or nuclear addressing that would be expected from the full-length protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed localization patterns of certain IDRs.

claim: Some IDRs play a functional role in protein localization.
source: This result suggests that these particular IDRs play a functional role in protein localization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed localization patterns.

claim: In the majority of cases (73/75), IDRs alone are insufficient to drive the subnuclear clustering observed in fluorescently tagged TFs in the embryo.
source: The nuclear uniformity of the majority of the IDRs in S2 cells suggested that in the majority of cases (73/75), IDRs alone are insufficient to drive the subnuclear clustering that we observe in fluorescently tagged TFs in the embryo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the S2 cell imaging data.

claim: Three of the nine full-length proteins, CG10321, Spps, and CG31510, showed notable subnuclear clustering relative to their corresponding IDR alone in S2 cells.
source: Three of the nine full-length proteins, CG10321, Spps, and CG31510, showed notable subnuclear clustering relative to their corresponding IDR alone (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: CG10321 encodes an 855 amino acid DNA-binding protein containing a zinc finger-associated domain and a cluster of C2H2-type zinc fingers.
source: The gene CG10321 encodes an 855 amino acid DNA-binding protein containing a zinc finger-associated domain and a cluster of C2H2-type zinc fingers (Gebali et al., 2019; Krystel and Ayyanathan, 2013; Letunic et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gebali et al., 2019; Krystel and Ayyanathan, 2013; Letunic et al., 2015.

claim: CG10321 is expressed throughout embryonic development and the Drosophila life cycle.
source: Though it is largely uncharacterized, it is expressed throughout embryonic development and the Drosophila life cycle (Brown et al., 2014) and is predicted to act as a transcriptional regulator (Gaudet et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2014.

claim: CG10321 is predicted to act as a transcriptional regulator.
source: Though it is largely uncharacterized, it is expressed throughout embryonic development and the Drosophila life cycle (Brown et al., 2014) and is predicted to act as a transcriptional regulator (Gaudet et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gaudet et al., 2011.

claim: Spps encodes a zinc finger DNA-binding protein that binds to Polycomb group response elements.
source: Sp1-like factor for pairing sensitive-silencing (Spps) encodes a zinc finger DNA-binding protein that has been shown to bind to Polycomb group response elements and to potentially play a role in recruiting Polycomb repressive complexes to these sites (Brown and Kassis, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brown and Kassis, 2010.

claim: Spps potentially plays a role in recruiting Polycomb repressive complexes to Polycomb group response elements.
source: Sp1-like factor for pairing sensitive-silencing (Spps) encodes a zinc finger DNA-binding protein that has been shown to bind to Polycomb group response elements and to potentially play a role in recruiting Polycomb repressive complexes to these sites (Brown and Kassis, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brown and Kassis, 2010.

claim: Spps is expressed ubiquitously in the embryo and continues to be expressed throughout the larval and adult life cycle.
source: It is expressed ubiquitously in the embryo and continues to be expressed throughout the larval and adult life cycle (Brown et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2014.

claim: CG31510 is expressed throughout the Drosophila life cycle.
source: CG31510 is expressed throughout the Drosophila life cycle (Brown et al., 2014) and encodes an 1150 amino acid protein that is almost entirely uncharacterized.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2014.

claim: CG31510 encodes an 1150 amino acid protein that is almost entirely uncharacterized.
source: CG31510 is expressed throughout the Drosophila life cycle (Brown et al., 2014) and encodes an 1150 amino acid protein that is almost entirely uncharacterized.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the protein.

claim: CG31510 contains two predicted C2H2-type zinc fingers in addition to its disordered sequence.
source: Though it does not contain any annotated canonical DNA-binding domains, it contains two predicted C2H2-type zinc fingers (Gebali et al., 2019) in addition to its disordered sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gebali et al., 2019.

claim: The IDR from CG31510 appears to have nucleolar localization in S2 cells.
source: The IDR from CG31510 appears to have nucleolar localization, which is maintained in the full-length version, in addition to bright clusters throughout the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The nucleolar localization of the CG31510 IDR is maintained in the full-length version.
source: The IDR from CG31510 appears to have nucleolar localization, which is maintained in the full-length version, in addition to bright clusters throughout the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Amino acid sequences outside of the IDRs are necessary for the nuclear dynamics of CG10321, Spps, and CG31510.
source: The dramatic clustering of these full-length proteins relative to their IDRs alone suggests that amino acid sequences outside of the IDRs are necessary for the nuclear dynamics of these TFs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential clustering observed between IDRs and full-length proteins.

claim: The IDRs alone were largely homogenous within the nucleus in live NC14 embryos.
source: Similar to the results observed in S2 cells, the IDRs alone were largely homogenous within the nucleus (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The full-length TFs show a range of subnuclear localization patterns in live NC14 embryos.
source: In contrast to the IDRs alone, the full-length TFs show a range of subnuclear localization patterns, as well as expression levels (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Three of the nine TFs – CG10321, Spps, and CG31510 – show substantial subnuclear clustering in live NC14 embryos.
source: Three of the nine TFs – CG10321, Spps, and CG31510 – show substantial subnuclear clustering.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The imaging data from live embryos recapitulates the findings in S2 cells.
source: Taken together, the imaging data from live embryos recapitulates the findings in S2 cells, namely that the IDRs identified in this study are insufficient to drive the subnuclear clustering we observe for the full-length TFs.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the S2 cell and embryo imaging data.

claim: CG10321 forms bright foci that appear to localize around the edges of the nucleus in embryos.
source: In embryos, CG10321 forms bright foci that appear to localize around the edges of the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Spps shows many bright clusters throughout the nucleus in embryos.
source: Spps, despite fairly low overall expression levels, shows many bright clusters throughout the nucleus that we might expect from a DNA-binding TF.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Spps clusters correspond to sites of Polycomb-mediated silencing.
source: We hypothesize that these clusters correspond to sites of Polycomb-mediated silencing.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known function of Spps.

claim: CG31510 forms bright clusters which are oriented apically in the nuclei in embryos.
source: Finally, CG31510 forms bright clusters which are oriented apically in the nuclei, which are non-overlapping with the Histone 2Av signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The CG31510 clusters are non-overlapping with the Histone 2Av signal.
source: Finally, CG31510 forms bright clusters which are oriented apically in the nuclei, which are non-overlapping with the Histone 2Av signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The nucleolus forms on the apical side of NC14 nuclei.
source: This is consistent with the formation of the nucleolus on the apical side of NC14 nuclei (Falahati et al., 2016), and therefore may recapitulate the nucleolar localization observed for both the IDR and full-length CG31510 protein in S2 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Falahati et al., 2016.

claim: The apical localization of CG31510 may recapitulate the nucleolar localization observed in S2 cells.
source: This is consistent with the formation of the nucleolus on the apical side of NC14 nuclei (Falahati et al., 2016), and therefore may recapitulate the nucleolar localization observed for both the IDR and full-length CG31510 protein in S2 cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed localization pattern.

claim: The IDR of Brk showed one or two bright foci of subnuclear localization in the embryo.
source: In the embryo, the IDR of Brk showed one or two bright foci of subnuclear localization (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The Brk IDR foci correspond to the HLB.
source: We suspected that these foci corresponded to the HLB.
evidence: This is speculation that was subsequently tested experimentally.

claim: The HLB forms around the histone gene cluster.
source: The HLB forms around the histone gene cluster, where factors required for the replication-coupled transcription and processing of histone mRNAs are concentrated (reviewed in Marzluff et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marzluff et al., 2008.

claim: Multi sex combs (mxc) is a homeotic gene and structural component of the HLB.
source: To test whether the Brk IDR foci corresponded to the HLB, we generated a fly line expressing an mRuby3-tagged multi sex combs (mxc), a homeotic gene and structural component of the HLB (White et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to White et al., 2011.

claim: The Brk IDR shows very strong co-localization with Mxc within the HLB.
source: We imaged embryos expressing both the fluorescently tagged IDR from Brk and Mxc and found very strong co-localization within the HLB (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The specialized localization of the Brk IDR indicates that IDRs can play a role in concentrating factors within the nucleus.
source: This specialized localization of the Brk IDR indicates that IDRs can play a role in concentrating factors within the nucleus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed HLB localization of the Brk IDR.

claim: IDR-mediated concentration of factors within the nucleus is not a common function of IDRs in general.
source: However, our screen demonstrates that this is not a common function of IDRs in general.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fact that only one IDR showed this behavior.

claim: The Brk TF is not known to be associated with the HLB.
source: The Brk TF is not known to be associated with the HLB, and the full-length Brk protein does not appear to have this localization pattern (Figure 4B and Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of Brk function and imaging data.

claim: The full-length Brk protein does not appear to have HLB localization.
source: The Brk TF is not known to be associated with the HLB, and the full-length Brk protein does not appear to have this localization pattern (Figure 4B and Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 4B and 5.

claim: The HLB localization of the Brk IDR could be the result of DNA binding to the histone locus.
source: However, as the Brk IDR is the only IDR in our panel that also contains the DNA-binding domain, the HLB localization could also be the result of DNA binding to the histone locus.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of HLB localization.

claim: The transgenic TFs are expressed ubiquitously in the embryo.
source: The transgenic TFs are expressed ubiquitously in the embryo and with a brighter fluorophore than eGFP, allowing for more effective imaging.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the transgenic constructs.

claim: The transgenic TFs showed a range of nuclear expression levels that are similar to the endogenous proteins.
source: Despite all of the constructs being expressed from the same promoter, the transgenic TFs showed a range of nuclear expression levels that are similar to the endogenous proteins (Figure 5), indicating post-transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The range of expression levels in transgenic TFs indicates post-transcriptional regulation.
source: Despite all of the constructs being expressed from the same promoter, the transgenic TFs showed a range of nuclear expression levels that are similar to the endogenous proteins (Figure 5), indicating post-transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that proteins expressed from the same promoter have different expression levels.

claim: The transgenic TFs reproduce the subnuclear clustering patterns of the endogenous TFs.
source: The transgenic TFs reproduce the subnuclear clustering patterns of the endogenous TFs, but the brighter mNeonGreen fluorophore and ubiquitous spatial expression in the embryo allows for several additional observations.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing imaging data in Figures 4B and 5.

claim: Rib shows fine-scale clustering that was not visible when the protein was tagged at the endogenous locus.
source: Rib shows fine-scale clustering that was not visible when the protein was tagged at the endogenous locus.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing imaging data in Figures 4B and 5.

claim: Brk and Disco both appear to be associated with chromatin.
source: And finally, Brk and Disco both appear to be associated with chromatin.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Four of the TFs, Rib, CG10321, CG13287, and Tgo, had severely reduced nuclear expression when the IDR was deleted.
source: Four of the TFs, Rib, CG10321, CG13287, and Tgo, had severely reduced nuclear expression when the IDR was deleted (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The reduced nuclear expression of IDR deletion constructs is possibly the result of the loss of a nuclear localization signal that resides within the IDR sequence.
source: This is possibly the result of the loss of a nuclear localization signal that resides within the IDR sequence.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of reduced expression.

claim: The most strongly clustering TFs in the set, CG10321, Spps, and CG31510, maintain their subnuclear clustering behavior with the IDRs deleted.
source: However, the most strongly clustering TFs in the set, CG10321, Spps, and CG31510, maintain their subnuclear clustering behavior with the IDRs deleted.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Even with drastically reduced expression, the clusters in CG10321 are still visible when the IDR is deleted.
source: Indeed, even with drastically reduced expression, the clusters in CG10321 are still visible.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Brk and Disco retain their chromatin localization with their IDRs deleted.
source: Brk and Disco also retain their chromatin localization with their IDRs deleted.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The IDRs are not necessary for the clustering behavior of the full-length TFs.
source: These results demonstrate that the IDRs are not necessary for the clustering behavior of the full-length TFs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the IDR deletion imaging data.

claim: Brk is expressed in a ventrolateral stripe in the embryo.
source: Both are expressed in a specific subset of nuclei and absent elsewhere in the embryo, with Brk expressed in a ventrolateral stripe (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and Disco in the posterior (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Disco is expressed in the posterior of the embryo.
source: Both are expressed in a specific subset of nuclei and absent elsewhere in the embryo, with Brk expressed in a ventrolateral stripe (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and Disco in the posterior (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There are no significant differences in subnuclear distribution of Brk and Disco IDR deletion constructs in nuclei where the endogenous proteins are absent.
source: We observe no significant differences in subnuclear distribution in nuclei where the endogenous proteins are absent, suggesting these TFs can maintain their subnuclear localization with their IDRs deleted and without interaction with the endogenous full-length protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Brk and Disco TFs can maintain their subnuclear localization with their IDRs deleted and without interaction with the endogenous full-length protein.
source: We observe no significant differences in subnuclear distribution in nuclei where the endogenous proteins are absent, suggesting these TFs can maintain their subnuclear localization with their IDRs deleted and without interaction with the endogenous full-length protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that IDR deletion constructs behave the same in regions with and without endogenous protein.

claim: IDRs have been implicated in driving liquid-liquid phase separation, promoting the formation of a diverse array of nuclear condensates.
source: IDRs have indeed been implicated in driving liquid-liquid phase separation, promoting the formation of a diverse array of nuclear condensates (Elbaum-Garfinkle et al., 2015; Nott et al., 2015; Strom et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Elbaum-Garfinkle et al., 2015; Nott et al., 2015; Strom et al., 2017.

claim: There is growing evidence that IDRs are involved in the formation of transcriptional condensates at promoters.
source: There is also growing evidence that IDRs are involved in the formation of transcriptional condensates at promoters (Boija et al., 2018; Chong et al., 2018; Cho et al., 2018; Sabari et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boija et al., 2018; Chong et al., 2018; Cho et al., 2018; Sabari et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2020.

claim: The role of IDR-mediated phase separation in transcription activation has been called into question.
source: More recently, however, the role of IDR-mediated phase separation in transcription activation has been called into question, given the highly dynamic nature of TF hub formation and the fact that true liquid-liquid phase separation is generally observed at concentrations far above those observed for nuclear TFs (Chong et al., 2022; Ferrie et al., 2022; McSwiggen et al., 2019; Trojanowski et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chong et al., 2022; Ferrie et al., 2022; McSwiggen et al., 2019; Trojanowski et al., 2022.

claim: True liquid-liquid phase separation is generally observed at concentrations far above those observed for nuclear TFs.
source: More recently, however, the role of IDR-mediated phase separation in transcription activation has been called into question, given the highly dynamic nature of TF hub formation and the fact that true liquid-liquid phase separation is generally observed at concentrations far above those observed for nuclear TFs (Chong et al., 2022; Ferrie et al., 2022; McSwiggen et al., 2019; Trojanowski et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chong et al., 2022; Ferrie et al., 2022; McSwiggen et al., 2019; Trojanowski et al., 2022.

claim: IDRs are neither necessary nor sufficient to drive the subnuclear clustering of TFs.
source: Here, we have shown that IDRs are neither necessary nor sufficient to drive the subnuclear clustering of TFs, results which demonstrate that clustering is not an emergent behavior of IDRs, and broadly rule out IDRs as major contributors to subnuclear clustering of TFs into functional hubs.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on all the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Clustering is not an emergent behavior of IDRs.
source: Here, we have shown that IDRs are neither necessary nor sufficient to drive the subnuclear clustering of TFs, results which demonstrate that clustering is not an emergent behavior of IDRs, and broadly rule out IDRs as major contributors to subnuclear clustering of TFs into functional hubs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing IDRs don't drive clustering.

claim: IDRs are not major contributors to subnuclear clustering of TFs into functional hubs.
source: Here, we have shown that IDRs are neither necessary nor sufficient to drive the subnuclear clustering of TFs, results which demonstrate that clustering is not an emergent behavior of IDRs, and broadly rule out IDRs as major contributors to subnuclear clustering of TFs into functional hubs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Almost all IDRs (73/75) were insufficient to drive protein clustering on their own in cultured S2 cells.
source: A functional imaging screen of 75 IDRs from Drosophila TFs revealed that almost all (73/75) were insufficient to drive protein clustering on their own in cultured S2 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the S2 cell imaging screen data.

claim: Several full-length TFs do cluster in S2 cells.
source: This finding was further supported by the fact that several full-length TFs do cluster in the same cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data of full-length TFs in S2 cells.

claim: TFs with their IDRs deleted still follow the same clustering patterns as their full-length counterparts.
source: Finally, we demonstrated that IDRs are dispensable for the subnuclear clustering that we observe, as TFs with their IDRs deleted still follow the same clustering patterns as their full-length counterparts.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data of IDR deletion constructs.

claim: TF hub formation may be more dependent on DNA binding than IDR-IDR interactions.
source: However, the coupling of the IDR and DNA-binding domain in this protein raises the possibility that TF hub formation is more dependent on DNA binding than IDR-IDR interactions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that the Brk IDR contains the DNA-binding domain.

claim: Bulk confocal imaging may be limiting in the types of nuclear dynamics that can be observed.
source: This approach, while conducive to a high-throughput investigation of many proteins, may be limiting in the types of nuclear dynamics that we can observe.
evidence: This is a discussion of the limitations of the experimental approach.

claim: The clustering observed in this study may be hubs that are stably bound to chromatin.
source: These findings leave open the possibility that the clustering that we are observing in this study are hubs that are stably bound to chromatin, and our bulk imaging approach is insufficient to observe more transient interactions between IDRs alone.
evidence: This is speculation about what the observed clustering represents.

claim: Bulk imaging approach may be insufficient to observe more transient interactions between IDRs alone.
source: These findings leave open the possibility that the clustering that we are observing in this study are hubs that are stably bound to chromatin, and our bulk imaging approach is insufficient to observe more transient interactions between IDRs alone.
evidence: This is speculation about the limitations of the imaging approach.

claim: IDRs can adopt different conformations depending on the intramolecular interactions that they have with adjacent folded domains.
source: Recent studies investigating the interplay between IDRs and adjacent folded domains in the same protein have shown IDRs can adopt different conformations depending on the intramolecular interactions that they have with adjacent folded domains, and their conformation is influenced by their position within a protein (Taneja and Holehouse, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Taneja and Holehouse, 2021.

claim: IDR conformation is influenced by their position within a protein.
source: Recent studies investigating the interplay between IDRs and adjacent folded domains in the same protein have shown IDRs can adopt different conformations depending on the intramolecular interactions that they have with adjacent folded domains, and their conformation is influenced by their position within a protein (Taneja and Holehouse, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Taneja and Holehouse, 2021.

claim: IDRs flanking folded binding domains can influence their binding affinity in protein-protein interactions.
source: Recent evidence has also shown that IDRs flanking folded binding domains can influence their binding affinity in protein-protein interactions, and may modulate the specificity of interaction networks (Karlsson et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Karlsson et al., 2022.

claim: IDRs may modulate the specificity of interaction networks.
source: Recent evidence has also shown that IDRs flanking folded binding domains can influence their binding affinity in protein-protein interactions, and may modulate the specificity of interaction networks (Karlsson et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Karlsson et al., 2022.

claim: IDRs play roles in modulating DNA-binding specificity and affinity of TFs via intramolecular interactions with DNA-binding domains.
source: IDRs have also been shown to play roles in modulating DNA-binding specificity and affinity of TFs via intramolecular interactions with DNA-binding domains (Baughman et al., 2022; He et al., 2019; Krois et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baughman et al., 2022; He et al., 2019; Krois et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2009.

claim: The effects of a given IDR may be specialized and context-dependent, rather than generalizable across all IDRs.
source: These studies suggest that the effects of a given IDR may be specialized and context-dependent, rather than generalizable across all IDRs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature about IDR functions.
